candidate.title: PARTE
candidate.scope: The complete central PARTE workflow in the assigned Illumina poster crop: Parallel analysis of RNA structures with temperature elevation. Poly(A) RNA is allocated to the two depicted temperature conditions, probed with RNase V1, randomly fragmented, and converted to separate cDNA products. The left yellow-highlighted hairpin icon illustrates the named assay; it is not a labeled material-processing operation. The upper PARS/dsRNA-Seq and lower Frag-seq rows are neighboring, partly clipped catalogue workflows, not alternatives within the PARTE row. Their enzymes and controls are therefore not PARTE operations or additional targets. This is a two-condition schematic, not the complete five-temperature implementation in the cited paper. The Illumina catalogue provenance does not establish the original sequencing platform; Wan et al. explicitly used SOLiD. The drawn endpoint is cDNA; no adapter construction, amplification, sequencing, or analysis block is drawn.

states.label: PolyA RNA
features: RNA substrate with secondary structure, shown as two hairpins; not cDNA or a probe product.
Poly(A)-enriched RNA is the depicted starting material. The paper describes extracted yeast RNA folded in vitro; the schematic does not depict extraction or poly(A) selection as a local operation.

operations.label: Parallel temperature branches (75°C / 25°C)
operations.description: Allocate the common poly(A) RNA substrate to independent upper and lower temperature-condition routes. This records the branching architecture, not a claim that the original experiment performed one particular physical split after a shared folding treatment.
operations.information_effect: Temperature identity is retained by separate physical sample routes to separate cDNA endpoints. No barcode, physical mixture, or joint library is depicted.

evidence.locator: [b00009], Results: RNA folded at 23 and 30°C; 30°C pool split for elevated-temperature samples
evidence.quote: The RNA pool was folded in vitro at 23 and 30°C, and the 30°C pool i s split and shifted to 30, 37, 55, or 75°C for five m inutes.

operations.label: RNase V1 digestion at different temperatures
operations.description: Probe this branch’s poly(A) RNA at 75°C with RNase V1. The shorter hairpin is open in the upper drawing while the longer stem remains structured. Cleavage converts structured RNA substrate into fragments with the depicted 5′P/3′OH ends; the enzyme icons are catalysts, not material products.
operations.mechanism: RNase V1 cleaves double-stranded RNA regions accessible under the probing condition. The paper experimentally checks double-stranded specificity through 75°C; the cartoon is a local susceptibility illustration, not an exhaustive list of all paired bases.
operations.information_effect: Cleavage-site identity is physically associated with RNA fragment sequence and its nuclease-generated end. Comparing mapped cleavage signals across conditions supports local pairing/structural-stability inference; a single cleavage is not direct evidence of the pairing partner.

evidence.locator: PARTE hot branch: 75°C label, RNA folding icon, RNase V1 catalyst, arrow to RNA fragments with 5′ phosphate ends
[b00009], Results: double-stranded specificity of RNase V1 and temperature-dependent probing
evidence.quote: RNA footprinting with RNase V1 of the well known, structured domains of the Tetrahymena ribozyme (Guo et al., 2004) revealed that RNase V1 retains its double-stranded specificity up to 75°C, and comparable footprinting results are obtained at different temperatures by correspondingly shorter incubation times with the enzyme to maintain single-hit kinetics (Fig. S1).

operations.label: Random fragmentation
operations.description: Shorten the RNA fragments from this temperature-specific RNase V1 digest. The output explicitly contains 5′P termini inherited from the digest and new 5′OH termini; keep the drawn 3′OH labels without assigning an unshown fragmentation reagent or detailed chemical mechanism.
operations.information_effect: Adds RNA breaks that are distinct from the structure-probing cuts. A fragment retaining the nuclease-created 5′P end preserves that cleavage boundary; a newly generated 5′OH end alone is not evidence of an RNase V1 cut.

evidence.locator: PARTE hot branch: 5′P RNA fragments → Random fragmentation → shorter 5′P- and 5′OH-bearing RNA fragments with 3′OH labels

operations.label: Reverse transcription
operations.description: Copy RNA from this branch’s fragmented material into complementary DNA. The purple/blue line pair illustrates the RNA-templated intermediate, and the following arrow terminates at the blue-only cDNA product. These are kept within the broad reverse-transcription-to-product block; the diagram supplies no separate RNA-removal reaction. The intervening library-construction interface is compressed: no end-selection, adapter, or primer mechanism is specified.
operations.mechanism: RNA-templated synthesis of complementary DNA, as named by the source caption. Purple denotes RNA elsewhere in the row and the terminal blue line is labeled cDNA; the intervening pair is therefore interpreted as RNA with its DNA copy, without assigning detailed strand-processing chemistry.
operations.information_effect: Transfers RNA sequence information to the DNA readout carrier; the physical 5′P/5′OH end-group distinction is not itself copied as RNA chemistry onto cDNA. The primary paper establishes that cloned-fragment reads map RNase V1 cleavage sites. Comparing temperature-specific cleavage signals supports inference of local structural stability and relative melting transitions. Increased signal can also reflect accessibility or redistribution of sampling as other structures melt. PARTE does not directly identify pairing partners, establish a unique full fold, or guarantee recovery of native protein-dependent and co-transcriptional structures. The exact cloning interface that preserves cleavage-end identity is unshown; no preferential capture chemistry is asserted here. These are readout interpretations, not extra depicted sequencing or analysis operations.
